title_en: Notice of the Supreme People's Court on Issuing the 34th Batch of Guiding Cases
ruling_gist_en: An online streamer who violates an agreed exclusive cooperation clause by engaging in similar business on other platforms without the live streaming platform's consent shall bear liability for breach of contract in accordance with the law. Where the online streamer claims that the liquidated damages stipulated in the contract are obviously excessive and requests a reduction, and where the actual losses are difficult to determine, the people's court may, based on the characteristics of the live streaming industry, take the actual income received by the streamer from the platform as a reference basis, and reasonably determine the amount by considering factors such as the platform's upfront investment, platform traffic, and the individual commercial value of the streamer.
full_text_en:
Supreme People's Court

Notice on Issuing the 34th Batch of Guiding Cases

Fa [2022] No. 240

Higher People's Courts of all provinces, autonomous regions, and municipalities directly under the Central Government; the Military Court of the People's Liberation Army; and the Production and Construction Corps Branch of the Higher People's Court of Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region:

Upon deliberation and decision by the Judicial Committee of the Supreme People's Court, the following three cases (Guiding Cases No. 189-191), including the dispute over contract between Shanghai Panda Interactive Entertainment Culture Co., Ltd. v. Li Cen and Kunshan Boaiyou Information Technology Co., Ltd., are hereby issued as the 34th batch of guiding cases for reference in adjudicating similar cases.

December 8, 2022

Guiding Case No. 189

Shanghai Panda Interactive Entertainment Culture Co., Ltd. v. Li Cen and Kunshan Boaiyou Information Technology Co., Ltd. — dispute over contract

(Deliberated and adopted by the Judicial Committee of the Supreme People's Court, issued on December 8, 2022)

Keywords: civil / dispute over contract / adjustment of liquidated damages / internet streamer

Ruling Gist

An internet streamer who violates an agreed exclusive cooperation clause and engages in similar business on other platforms without the consent of the live-streaming platform shall bear liability for breach of contract in accordance with the law. Where the streamer claims that the liquidated damages agreed in the contract are obviously excessive and requests a reduction, and the actual loss is difficult to determine, the people's court may, based on the characteristics of the internet live-streaming industry, take the actual income obtained by the streamer from the platform as a reference basis, and reasonably decide the amount by taking into account factors such as the platform's initial investment, platform traffic, and the streamer's individual commercial value.

Relevant Legal Provisions

Article 585 of the Civil Code of the People's Republic of China (Article 114 of the Contract Law of the People's Republic of China, which came into effect on October 1, 1999, applied in this case)

Basic Facts

The defendant Li Cen was originally a game streamer on the Panda live-streaming platform founded by the plaintiff Shanghai Panda Interactive Entertainment Culture Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Panda Company). The defendant Kunshan Boaiyou Information Technology Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Boaiyou Company) was Li Cen's agency company. On February 28, 2018, Panda Company, Boaiyou Company, and Li Cen signed the "Exclusive Cooperation Agreement for Streamers" (hereinafter referred to as the "Cooperation Agreement"), stipulating that Li Cen would exclusively conduct first-person perspective live game streaming and game commentary for "PlayerUnknown's Battlegrounds" on the Panda live-streaming platform. The breach of contract clause in the agreement provided that during the term of the agreement, if Boaiyou Company or Li Cen, without the consent of Panda Company, unilaterally terminated this agreement, or engaged in identical or similar cooperation on a competing live-streaming platform, or authorized any third party to use the live-streaming videos already published on the Panda platform, it would constitute a fundamental breach of contract. In such a case, Boaiyou Company should pay the following compensation to the Panda live-streaming platform: (1) the total cooperation fees paid by Panda Company to Li Cen for live-streaming cooperation with the Panda platform under this agreement and prior to this agreement; (2) RMB 50 million; and (3) the training fees and promotional resource fees invested by Panda Company for Li Cen. Streamer Li Cen assumed joint and several liability to Panda Company for this. The cooperation term agreed in the contract was one year, from March 1, 2018 to February 28, 2019.

On June 1, 2018, Boaiyou Company sent a payment reminder to Panda Company, demanding payment of the overdue cooperation fees for two months owed to Li Cen. As of June 4, 2018, Panda Company had paid a total of RMB 1,111,661 in cooperation fees for Li Cen's live-streaming from February 2017 to March 2018.

On June 27, 2018, Li Cen posted a microblog stating that he would lead his live-streaming team to the Douyu live-streaming platform for broadcasts, and announced the broadcast time and room number. On June 29, 2018, Li Cen made his first broadcast on the Douyu live-streaming platform. Boaiyou Company also published the link to Li Cen's live-stream room on the Douyu platform on its official WeChat public account. According to a public report from the "Tencent Games" microblog news: "BIU Brother Lei (Li Cen) is a pioneer of national console game live-streaming programs, a nationally renowned online game live-streaming celebrity streamer, and also an original creator on the Youku game channel, with over 200,000 followers and 50 million clicks on Youku..."

On August 24, 2018, Panda Company initiated a lawsuit in the people's court, requesting that the two defendants continue to perform the exclusive cooperation agreement, immediately cease live-streaming activities on other platforms, and pay corresponding liquidated damages. During the first-instance trial, Panda Company adjusted its claim to request that the two defendants pay the plaintiff liquidated damages of RMB 3 million. Boaiyou Company did not agree with Panda Company's claim and filed a counterclaim: 1. Requesting confirmation that the "Cooperation Agreement" signed by Panda Company, Boaiyou Company, and Li Cen on February 28, 2018 was terminated on June 28, 2018; 2. Requesting that Panda Company pay Boaiyou Company the cooperation fees between April 2018 and June 2018 in the amount of RMB 224,923.32; 3. Requesting that Panda Company pay Boaiyou Company attorney's fees of RMB 20,000.

Judgment

The Shanghai Jing'an District People's Court rendered a civil judgment (2018) Hu 0106 Min Chu No. 31513 on September 16, 2019: 1. Boaiyou Company shall pay Panda Company liquidated damages of RMB 2,600,000 within ten days from the effective date of the judgment; 2. Li Cen shall assume joint and several liability for the above payment obligation of Boaiyou Company; 3. Panda Company shall pay Boaiyou Company cooperation fees of RMB 186,640.10 for the period from April 2018 to June 2018 within ten days from the effective date of the judgment; 4. All other counterclaims of Boaiyou Company are rejected. Li Cen appealed against the first-instance judgment. The Shanghai Second Intermediate People's Court rendered a civil judgment (2020) Hu 02 Min Zhong No. 562 on November 12, 2020: Appeal dismissed; original judgment affirmed.

Reasoning

The effective judgment of the court held that:

First, based on the facts ascertained in this case, Panda Company, Boaiyou Company, and Li Cen voluntarily established a contractual legal relationship by signing the "Cooperation Agreement," rather than the labor relationship claimed by Li Cen. The "Cooperation Agreement" was the true expression of intention of the three parties, did not violate the mandatory provisions of laws and regulations, and should be deemed valid. All parties should comply with it as agreed. According to the liquidated damages clause of the "Cooperation Agreement," the rights and obligations of the three cooperating parties were detailed. The streamer's failure to obtain Panda Company's consent before streaming on a competing platform constituted a breach of contract and should bear liability for compensation.

Second, although Panda Company had performance defects, they did not constitute a fundamental breach of contract. Boaiyou Company and Li Cen could not rely on this as a reason to claim termination of the "Cooperation Agreement." Moreover, even in terms of the method of termination, a declaration of intent to terminate a contract should be clearly and unequivocally communicated to the other party in accordance with legal or agreed methods. Li Cen's "official announcement" posted on the microblog platform to unspecified persons or his direct streaming on other platforms could not be deemed as a clear declaration of intent to terminate the contract to Panda Company. Therefore, the claims of Li Cen and Boaiyou Company in the second instance that they had exercised their right to terminate the contract due to Panda Company's breach could not be established.

Third, where a party claims that the agreed liquidated damages are excessively high and requests a reduction, the actual loss should be taken as the basis, with comprehensive consideration of factors such as the performance of the contract, the degree of fault of the parties, and expected benefits, measured according to the principles of fairness and good faith. The application of the principles of fairness and good faith and the accurate determination of losses caused by the breach should fully consider the characteristics of the emerging internet live-streaming industry. Internet live-streaming platforms are enterprises that rely on the internet as a necessary medium and have streamers as core resources. In platform operations, they typically need to invest substantial upfront costs in bandwidth and streamers. The specific amount of loss caused to the live-streaming platform by a streamer's breach of contract by streaming on a third-party platform is difficult to quantify. Imposing excessively heavy burden of proof on internet live-streaming platforms would violate the principle of fairness. Therefore, the adjustment of liquidated damages in this case should consider the characteristics of internet live-streaming platforms and the foreseeability of Panda Company's costs and benefits when signing the contract. In this case, given the actual situation that streamer Li Cen enjoyed great popularity and had a high reputation in the game live-streaming industry, and taking into account his income, the remaining term of the contract, the breach and respective degree of fault of both parties, the quantifiable losses of Panda Company, the reduction of the agreed liquidated damages already made by Panda Company, the current status of Panda Company's platform, and other circumstances, in accordance with the principles of fairness and good faith and the balance of interests between the live-streaming platform and the individual streamer, the liquidated damages were appropriately adjusted to RMB 2.6 million.

(Judges of the effective judgment: He Yun, Zhang Mingliang, Shao Meilin)

Guiding Case No. 190

Wang Shan v. Wind Information Technology Co., Ltd. — dispute over non-competition restrictions

(Deliberated and adopted by the Judicial Committee of the Supreme People's Court, issued on December 8, 2022)

Keywords: civil / non-competition restrictions / review criteria / business scope

Ruling Gist

When adjudicating a dispute over non-competition restrictions, the people's court, in reviewing whether a worker's self-employment or new employing entity forms a competitive relationship with the original employing entity, should not only determine based on whether their legally registered business scopes overlap, but should also make a comprehensive judgment based on whether their actual business contents, service objects or product audiences, and corresponding markets overlap. Where a worker provides evidence proving that the actual business content, service objects or product audiences, and corresponding markets of his or her self-employment or new employing entity are different from those of the original employing entity, and claims that no competitive relationship exists, the people's court shall support such claim.

Relevant Legal Provisions

Articles 23 and 24 of the Labor Contract Law of the People's Republic of China

Basic Facts

Wang Shan started working at Wind Information Technology Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Wind Company) on July 2, 2018. The parties signed a labor contract with a term from July 2, 2018 to August 31, 2021, stipulating that Wang Shan would work in the position of intelligent data analysis, with a monthly base salary of RMB 4,500 and a position allowance of RMB 15,500, totaling RMB 20,000.

On July 23, 2019, Wang Shan and Wind Company signed the "Non-Competition Agreement," which specified the non-compete acts, non-compete period, non-compete compensation, and other terms. On July 27, 2020, Wang Shan filled in the "Resignation Application Form" and terminated the labor contract with Wind Company for personal reasons.

On August 5, 2020, Wind Company sent Wang Shan a "Reminder Letter on Non-Competition Restrictions," stating: "You (i.e., Wang Shan) are required to assume non-competition obligations from the date of resignation, July 27, 2020. You shall not work or hold positions within the scope of competing enterprises. Starting this month, we will pay you non-competition compensation. Within 10 days after receiving the non-competition compensation, please provide the labor contract signed with the new employer and social security records. If you are unemployed, please provide a certificate of your employment status issued by the sub-district office or other state organs. If you violate the non-competition obligation or other obligations, please rectify within 10 days. If you continue to violate the non-competition agreement, the company has the right to demand that you bear liquidated damages again in accordance with the Non-Competition Agreement, with the standard for liquidated damages being RMB 200,000 or more, and you shall return all non-competition compensation paid by the company after your resignation..."

On October 12, 2020, Wind Company sent Wang Shan a "Legal Notice," again requesting Wang Shan to perform the non-competition obligations.

It was also ascertained that Wind Company's business scope includes: development and sales of computer software and hardware; technical development, transfer, consulting, and services in the field of computer professional technology and products.

Wang Shan joined Shanghai Bilibili Technology Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Bilibili Company) on August 6, 2020. According to its business license, the company's business scope includes: technical development, transfer, consulting, and services in the fields of information technology, computer software and hardware, and network technology, etc.

Wang Shan and Wind Company confirmed jointly: Wang Shan's non-compete period is from July 28, 2020 to July 27, 2022; Wind Company has paid Wang Shan non-competition compensation of RMB 6,796.92 for the period from July 28, 2020 to September 27, 2020.

On November 13, 2020, Wind Company applied for arbitration to the Shanghai Pudong New Area Labor and Personnel Dispute Arbitration Committee, requesting that Wang Shan: 1. Perform the non-competition obligations in accordance with the signed "Non-Competition Agreement"; 2. Return the non-competition compensation of RMB 6,796 paid for August and September 2020; 3. Pay liquidated damages for breach of non-competition restrictions of RMB 2 million. On February 25, 2021, the Arbitration Committee made an award: Wang Shan shall continue to perform the non-competition obligations in accordance with the signed "Non-Competition Agreement"; Wang Shan shall return to Wind Company the non-competition compensation of RMB 6,796 paid for August and September 2020; Wang Shan shall pay Wind Company liquidated damages for breach of non-competition restrictions of RMB 2 million. Wang Shan, dissatisfied with the arbitration award, filed a lawsuit with the court.

Judgment

The Shanghai Pudong New Area People's Court rendered a civil judgment (2021) Hu 0115 Min Chu No. 35993 on June 29, 2021: 1. Wang Shan shall continue to perform the non-competition obligations with Wind Company; 2. Wang Shan shall return to Wind Company the non-competition compensation of RMB 6,796 for the period from July 28, 2020 to September 27, 2020 within ten days from the effective date of the judgment; 3. Wang Shan shall pay Wind Company liquidated damages for breach of non-competition restrictions of RMB 240,000 within ten days from the effective date of the judgment. Wang Shan appealed against the first-instance judgment. The Shanghai First Intermediate People's Court rendered a civil judgment (2021) Hu 01 Min Zhong No. 12282 on January 26, 2022: 1. Affirm item 1 of the civil judgment (2021) Hu 0115 Min Chu No. 35993 of the Shanghai Pudong New Area People's Court; 2. Set aside items 2 and 3 of the civil judgment (2021) Hu 0115 Min Chu No. 35993 of the Shanghai Pudong New Area People's Court; 3. The appellant Wang Shan is not required to return to the appellee Wind Company the non-competition compensation of RMB 6,796 for the period from July 28, 2020 to September 27, 2020; 4. The appellant Wang Shan is not required to pay the appellee Wind Company liquidated damages for breach of non-competition restrictions of RMB 2 million.

Reasoning

The effective judgment of the court held that: Regarding whether Wang Shan violated the non-competition agreement. The so-called non-competition restriction means that a worker who owes a duty of confidentiality to the original employer shall not, within an agreed period after resignation, produce, operate on his or her own, or produce or operate for others, any products or business that are competitive with those of the original employer, and shall not work for an employer that has a competitive relationship with the original employer. The purpose of establishing the non-competition system is to prevent a worker from using the trade secrets of the original employer that he or she knows to seek benefits for himself or herself or for others, thereby seizing the market share of the original employer and causing losses to the original employer. Therefore, the core factor in determining whether a worker has violated the non-competition agreement is to assess whether a competitive relationship has been formed between the original employer and the worker's self-employment or the employer he or she has joined.

It should be noted that precisely because the non-competition system protects the rights and interests of the employer while imposing certain restrictions on the worker's right to employment, when reviewing whether a worker has violated the non-competition obligation, it is necessary to comprehensively and objectively review whether a competitive relationship has been formed between the worker's self-employment or the company he or she has joined and the original employer. On one hand, considering that in practice there are often inconsistencies between the registered business items and the actual business items of an enterprise, and on the other hand, considering that the categories of business scope registered are broad categories divided by the industrial and commercial authorities, the review of such competitive relationships should not be confined to the business scope registered in the business license; otherwise, it may cause unfairness to either the worker or the employer. Therefore, in a specific case, the review can also be conducted from multiple perspectives, such as whether the actual business content of the two enterprises overlaps, whether the service objects or the audiences of the products produced overlap, and whether the corresponding markets overlap, so as to restore the truth of the facts, thereby balancing the interests of the employer and the worker to achieve an ultimate equilibrium.

In this case, Wind Company's business scope includes development and sales of computer software and hardware, technical development, transfer, consulting, and services in the field of computer professional technology and products. Bilibili Company's business scope includes technical development, transfer, consulting, and services in the fields of information technology, computer software and hardware, network technology, etc. Comparing the business scopes of the two companies, there is indeed some overlap. However, when internet companies register, their business scopes often include software and hardware development, technical consulting, technical transfer, and technical services. If the judgment is based solely on this, it would obviously create significant obstacles for internet workers, especially software engineers, to find re-employment, cause a huge waste of social human resources, and also run counter to the legislative intent of the non-competition system. Therefore, when determining whether a competitive relationship exists, it is also necessary to comprehensively evaluate factors such as the actual business content and the audience of the company.

In this case, Wang Shan adduced evidence to prove that Wind Information Co., Ltd. (hereinafter "Wind Company") claimed on its Wind Financial mobile terminal that the Wind Financial terminal is the choice of hundreds of thousands of financial professionals and the best production tool and platform for China's financial industry. Furthermore, the official website of Wind Company introduces that "Wind Company (Wind) is a leading financial data, information, and software service enterprise in Mainland China, holding a leading position in the domestic financial information service industry. It is an indispensable and important partner for numerous securities companies, fund management companies, insurance companies, banks, investment companies, media, and other institutions. In the international market, Wind is also favored by many qualified foreign institutional investors approved by the China Securities Regulatory Commission. In addition, well-known financial academic research institutions and authoritative regulatory agencies are also Wind's clients; authoritative Chinese and English media, research reports, and academic papers frequently cite the data provided by Wind..." From this, it can be seen that Wind Company's current business model is primarily to provide financial information services, and its main audience is related financial institutions or financial academic research institutions. In contrast, as is well known, Bilibili Inc.'s main business is a cultural community and video platform, i.e., providing network space for users to upload videos and communicate. Its audience is broader, especially favored by young people. Comparing the two, there are significant differences in business models, corresponding markets, and audiences. Even ordinary people can easily discern the differences between them. Although Bilibili Inc. also ventures into areas such as gaming, music, and film and television, there is no evidence showing overlap with the financial information services operated by Wind Company. Under this premise, Wind Company's assertion that the two enterprises are in a competitive relationship solely based on the overlap of their registered business scopes has not fulfilled its burden of proof. Moreover, the key restricted enterprises listed in the appendix to Wind Company's non-competition agreement are all in the financial information industry, which sufficiently indicates that Wind Company itself also considers its main competitors to be financial information service enterprises. Therefore, the first-instance court's determination that Wang Shan's employment with Bilibili Inc. violated the non-competition agreement, solely based on the overlap of business scopes between Wind Company and Bilibili Inc., and its subsequent judgment ordering Wang Shan to return the non-competition compensation and pay liquidated damages for breach of the non-competition agreement, were somewhat improper.

Regarding the issue of whether Wang Shan should continue to perform the non-competition agreement. The non-competition agreement signed between Wang Shan and Wind Company contains no content that violates mandatory provisions of laws or regulations; therefore, the agreement is legally valid and binding on both parties. Since the agreement stipulates that the non-competition period between the parties is from July 28, 2020, to July 27, 2022, and it is currently still within that period, the first-instance court's judgment that both parties should continue to perform the non-competition agreement was not improper. Wang Shan's claim that he is not required to continue performing the non-competition agreement lacks a legal basis. It needs to be emphasized that, according to the non-competition agreement between the parties, Wang Shan should report his work status to Wind Company in a timely manner so that Wind Company can determine whether he has violated the agreement. The present dispute arose precisely because Wang Shan failed to fulfill his reporting obligation, leading to reasonable suspicion from Wind Company. When performing the non-competition agreement in the future, Wang Shan should abide by the stipulated obligations and perform the agreement in good faith.

(Judges of the Effective Judgment: Wang Qian, Zhou Yin, Zheng Donghe)

Guiding Case No. 191

Liu Caili v. Yingde City People's Government, Guangdong Province — administrative reconsideration dispute

(Adopted by the Judicial Committee of the Supreme People's Court on December 8, 2022)

Keywords

Administration; Administrative Reconsideration; Work-Related Injury Determination; Employer's Liability for Work-Related Injury Insurance

Ruling Gist

Where a construction enterprise, in violation of laws and regulations, subcontracts a project it has contracted to a natural person for actual construction, and that natural person suffers a work-related injury or death, and the social insurance administrative department, with reference to the relevant provisions of Article 3, paragraph 1 of the Provisions of the Supreme People's Court on Several Issues Concerning the Trial of Administrative Cases on Work-Related Injury Insurance, determines the construction enterprise as the unit bearing the liability for work-related injury insurance, the people's court shall support such determination.

Relevant Legal Provisions

Article 15 of the Regulations on Work-Related Injury Insurance

Basic Facts

On March 31, 2016, Zhu Zhanxiong signed a construction contract with Maoming Maonan Construction & Installation Group Co., Ltd. (hereinafter "Jian'an Company") for the Zhu Zhanxiong commercial-residential building project, with Zhu Zhanxiong as the employer and Jian'an Company as the contractor. A supplementary agreement stipulated that Jian'an Company would establish a dedicated account for workers' wages, with the account holder being Lu Haifeng. Subsequently, the construction approval procedures for the Zhu Zhanxiong commercial-residential building project were completed with Jian'an Company as the construction unit. The project involved was constructed by workers organized by Liang, with Lu Haifeng also participating in on-site management. The construction site gate, construction signage, and other conspicuous locations all indicated the project's contractor as Jian'an Company. It was also found that Jian'an Company had insured the project with group personal accident insurance for construction workers, with the policy stating 30 insured persons, but no list of names attached. On June 9, 2017, Liang and Lu Haifeng received a notice of inspection from the housing and construction department of Yingde City. The two, along with other workers at the site, waited for the inspection in a rented house. This rented house was leased by Liang and used for project meetings, work assignments, and wage distribution. At approximately 15:00 that day, Liang was found lying in the rented house, with the cause of death being sudden death.

Liu Caili, Liang's wife, applied to the Yingde City人力资源和社会保障 Bureau of Guangdong Province (hereinafter "Yingde City Human Resources and Social Security Bureau") for a work-related injury determination. The Yingde City Human Resources and Social Security Bureau issued the "Decision on Deeming Liang's Death as Equivalent to Work-Related Death" (hereinafter the "Deemed Work-Related Death Decision"), finding that Liang died from a sudden illness at the work site during working hours and within 48 hours, which falls under the circumstances specified in Article 15, paragraph 1, item 1 of the Regulations on Work-Related Injury Insurance, and deemed it equivalent to death from work-related injury. Jian'an Company disagreed and applied to the Yingde City People's Government, Guangdong Province (hereinafter "Yingde City Government") for administrative reconsideration. The Yingde City Government issued an "Administrative Reconsideration Decision," revoking the Deemed Work-Related Death Decision on the grounds that the facts were unclear, evidence insufficient, applicable legal basis erroneous, and procedure unlawful. Liu Caili disagreed and filed a lawsuit requesting the revocation of the Administrative Reconsideration Decision and the restoration of the validity of the Deemed Work-Related Death Decision.

Judgment

The Qingyuan Intermediate People's Court, Guangdong Province, rendered an administrative judgment on July 27, 2018 ((2018) Yue 18 Xing Chu No. 42), dismissing Liu Caili's claims. Liu Caili appealed. The High People's Court of Guangdong Province rendered an administrative judgment on September 29, 2019 ((2019) Yue Xing Zhong No. 390), dismissing the appeal and affirming the original judgment. Liu Caili applied to the Supreme People's Court for retrial. The Supreme People's Court issued an administrative ruling on November 9, 2020 ((2020) Zui Gao Fa Xing Shen No. 5851), granting retrial of this case. On April 27, 2021, the Supreme People's Court rendered an administrative judgment ((2021) Zui Gao Fa Xing Zai No. 1): 1. Reversing the administrative judgment of the High People's Court of Guangdong Province ((2019) Yue Xing Zhong No. 390); 2. Reversing the administrative judgment of the Qingyuan Intermediate People's Court, Guangdong Province ((2018) Yue 18 Xing Chu No. 42); 3. Annulling the Administrative Reconsideration Decision (Ying Fu Fu Jue [2018] No. 2) issued by the Yingde City Government; 4. Restoring the validity of the Deemed Work-Related Death Decision (Ying Ren She Gong Ren [2017] No. 194) issued by the Yingde City Human Resources and Social Security Bureau.

Reasoning

The Supreme People's Court holds that:

I. Jian'an Company should be the unit bearing the liability for work-related injury insurance

As a contracting unit with the qualification to employ workers, since it enjoys the rights of a contracting unit, it should also fulfill the obligations of a contracting unit. In terms of bearing liability for work-related injury insurance, although Jian'an Company did not directly sign a subcontract with Liang, it allowed Liang to use its qualifications and operate under its name. By reference to Article 4 of the Notice of the former Ministry of Labor and Social Security on Relevant Issues Concerning the Establishment of Labor Relations (Lao She Bu Fa [2005] No. 12), paragraph 7 of the Opinions of the Ministry of Human Resources and Social Security on Several Issues Concerning the Implementation of the Regulations on Work-Related Injury Insurance (Ren She Bu Fa [2013] No. 34, hereinafter "MOHRSS Opinions on Work-Related Injury Insurance"), and the spirit of items 4 and 5 of paragraph 1 of Article 3 of the Provisions of the Supreme People's Court on Several Issues Concerning the Trial of Administrative Cases on Work-Related Injury Insurance (hereinafter "Provisions on Administrative Cases on Work-Related Injury Insurance"), Jian'an Company may be deemed the unit bearing the liability for work-related injury insurance.

II. Jian'an Company should bear the liability for work-related injury insurance for Liang's death

The Yingde City Government and Jian'an Company argued that, according to relevant legal provisions, Liang was a "subcontractor" lacking the qualification to employ workers, and was neither a worker recruited by Jian'an Company nor an employee hired by it. Therefore, Jian'an Company should not bear the liability for work-related injury insurance for Liang's work-related injury death. In response, the Supreme People's Court holds that including a work-related injured or deceased "subcontractor" within the scope of work-related injury insurance, granting him the right to enjoy work-related injury insurance benefits, and requiring the contracting unit with the qualification to employ workers to bear the employer's liability for work-related injury insurance as required by law, is consistent with the original purpose of establishing the work-related injury insurance system and also conforms to the legislative intent of the Regulations on Work-Related Injury Insurance and related normative documents.

First, in the construction industry, the contracting unit with the qualification to employ workers bears the liability for work-related injury insurance for workers who are injured or die from work-related injuries on a project that was illegally subcontracted or sub-subcontracted, and this is not conditioned on the existence of a legal or de facto labor relationship. According to paragraph 7 of the MOHRSS Opinions on Work-Related Injury Insurance and Article 3 of the Provisions on Administrative Cases on Work-Related Injury Insurance, in order to protect the work-related injury insurance benefits of workers employed by organizations or natural persons lacking the qualification to employ workers in the construction industry, and to strengthen the tilted protection of workers and punishment of entities that illegally subcontract or sub-subcontract, the current work-related injury insurance system establishes a rule that a labor relationship between the injured or deceased worker and the contracting unit is presumed to be formed by legal fiction, i.e., the illegally subcontracting or sub-subcontracting contracting unit is directly deemed the employer and bears the liability for work-related injury insurance.

Second, including the "subcontractor" within the scope of work-related injury insurance is consistent with the development direction of work-related injury insurance in the construction field. According to the spirit of normative documents such as the Opinions of the General Office of the State Council on Promoting the Sustainable and Healthy Development of the Construction Industry (Guo Ban Fa [2017] No. 19) and the Notice of the General Office of the Ministry of Human Resources and Social Security on Further Improving the Work on Work-Related Injury Insurance in the Construction Industry (Ren She Ting Han [2017] No. 53), it is required to improve the work-related injury insurance participation policies suitable for the characteristics of the construction industry and vigorously expand the coverage of work-related injury insurance for construction enterprises. That is, according to the characteristics of the construction industry, construction enterprises should participate in work-related injury insurance as employers for relatively fixed employees; for workers who cannot participate in insurance as employers, especially migrant workers employed by construction projects, they should participate in insurance on a per-project basis. Therefore, including all laborers, including "subcontractors," in per-project work-related injury insurance and expanding the coverage of work-related injury insurance for construction enterprises is consistent with the development direction of the work-related injury insurance system in the construction field.

Third, including "subcontractors" within the scope of work-related injury insurance objects conforms to the legislative purpose of the work-related injury insurance system of "ensuring coverage for all who should be covered." The provision in the Regulations on Work-Related Injury Insurance regarding "all employees or hired workers of this unit" does not exclude special employing entities such as individual industrial and commercial households or "subcontractors" from participating in work-related injury insurance. In other words, neither the original intent of establishing the work-related injury insurance system nor the specific provisions of work-related injury insurance laws and regulations exclude or should exclude "subcontractors" from the scope of work-related injury insurance. As laborers, "subcontractors" are at the end of the interest chain in illegal subcontracting and sub-subcontracting behaviors; they participate in and bear the specific management work on the construction site, and some even directly participate in the specific construction. They may also suffer from injuries or death at work, during work hours, and due to work reasons. In terms of the work-related injury insurance system and liability for work-related injury insurance, there is no essential difference between the work-related injury death of a "subcontractor" and that of a construction worker employed by him. If the scope of application of the Regulations on Work-Related Injury Insurance is artificially limited by excluding "subcontractors" from the scope of work-related injury insurance, it would result in de facto inequality. Including special subjects such as "subcontractors" within the scope of work-related injury insurance is conducive to realizing the tilted protection of all laborers and demonstrating the superiority of the socialist work-related injury insurance system.

Finally, the legal liability of a "subcontractor" for illegally undertaking a project does not conflict with his right to participate in social insurance. According to Article 1 and Article 33 of the Social Insurance Law, work-related injury insurance, as an important component of the social insurance system, is implemented by the state through compulsory legislation. It is the state's social responsibility to employees and a basic right that employees should enjoy. The fact that a "subcontractor" illegally undertakes a project in violation of construction laws and regulations should not negate his right to enjoy social insurance. If a contracting unit uses its own name and qualifications to contract a construction project but allows a subject lacking the required qualifications to actually construct the project, and gains benefits from the illegal subcontracting, sub-subcontracting, or affiliated operation, it is consistent with the principle of fairness and justice for that contracting unit to bear the corresponding liability for work-related injury insurance. Of course, after the contracting unit bears the liability for work-related injury insurance according to law, it may, in accordance with legal provisions, seek recourse from the corresponding responsible party for the corresponding liability.

(Judges of the Effective Judgment: Geng Baojian, Song Chuxiao, Liu Aitao)
